title: How to compare prices from a photo
description: Learn how to check a product's price from a photo, verify the exact model, and compare real costs before buying with your iPhone.
summary: To compare prices from a photo, capture the product and its identifying details, use a photo price comparison app to find matches, then check the exact model and total cost. OLMA lets you start that search with your iPhone camera.

sections.title: Start with a photo that identifies the product
sections.html:
Standing in a shop with an unfamiliar product is a different problem from browsing a retailer's website. You may have a box and a shelf label, but no link to search. A photo can give you a starting point without typing a long product name.

Photograph the front of the packaging in good light. Include the brand, model name, and size where possible. If the price label is separate, make sure it belongs to that item. A label one shelf below the product can lead to a misleading comparison.

For electronics, find the model number on the box. For cosmetics, include the volume and formulation. For shoes, capture the model and version. The more distinctive the details, the easier it is to distinguish a real match from a lookalike.

sections.title: Check that the result is the same item
sections.html:
A product photo can be ambiguous. Two boxes may look almost identical while containing different generations, sizes, or accessories. Treat the first result as a candidate to verify.

  • Model: match the full identifier, including the suffix.
  • Variant: check capacity, pack count, size, and included accessories.
  • Condition: separate new products from used or refurbished ones.
  • Availability: an unavailable listing is not an offer you can buy.

If the match looks wrong, take a clearer photo of the identifying label or use the model number to search a retailer directly. An uncertain match is a reason to investigate, not proof that the shop is expensive.

sections.title: Turn the comparison into a buying decision
sections.html:
Suppose a shop asks $85 for headphones and an online listing shows $79. If delivery costs $8, the online total is $87 before any difference in tax. The smaller headline price does not win that comparison. This is an illustrative example, not a live offer.

Also consider whether you need the item today and how you would return it. A useful price check ends with an option you can actually buy on acceptable terms. Read how to tell whether a sale is a good deal for a fuller decision checklist.

title: How to tell if a sale is actually a good deal
description: Check whether a sale price is a real saving. Compare the same product, calculate the total cost, and look beyond the advertised discount.
summary: A sale is a good deal when the total price is competitive for the exact item you want, the seller and return terms suit you, and the purchase fits your plans. A large percentage off the advertised original price is not enough to establish value.

sections.title: Compare against available prices, not just the sale tag
sections.html:
A crossed-out price gives you one reference point: the number printed on the tag. It does not tell you what other shops charge today. Before reacting to “40% off,” find current offers for the same model and condition.

Consider a fictional coffee maker marked down from $150 to $90. That is a 40% reduction from the stated original price. But if another retailer sells the same machine for $85 with the same delivery and return terms, the sale is still $5 more expensive than the alternative.

This distinction matters when you are shopping quickly. A discount describes a change from a reference price. A comparison tells you which available option costs less.

sections.title: Write down the total cost of each option
sections.html:
Use the same basis for both offers: product price plus shipping, applicable tax, and required fees, minus discounts you actually qualify for. Do not count a future reward as an immediate reduction unless you would otherwise spend that reward.

Illustrative comparison for the same item; both options use the same hypothetical tax amount.
CostSale offerOther retailer
Product$90$85
Shipping$0$8
Tax$7$7
Total$97$100

With those delivery costs, the sale offer becomes $3 cheaper. If the other retailer offers free collection, the answer changes again. Compare the checkout route you will actually use.

sections.title: Check what you give up for the lower price
sections.html:
A final-sale item may be less useful than a returnable one if you are unsure about fit. A bundle may include accessories you already own. A cheaper version may have less storage than the model you intended to buy.

The FTC's online shopping guidance recommends checking total costs and the conditions attached to advertised deals. It also advises examining delivery and refund policies before purchasing.

Choose your tradeoffs deliberately. Paying a little more for a return option can make sense; paying for an unnecessary bundle to unlock a discount may not.

sections.title: Decide whether to buy, wait, or skip
sections.html:
• Buy: you planned to buy the item, verified the match, and found acceptable total cost and terms.
  • Wait: you have no urgent need and the current offers do not meet your target price.
  • Skip: the discount is the main reason you want something you had not planned to buy.

OLMA can help you start that check from a product photo while you are in a shop. Its verdict is a starting point for comparison, not a promise about future prices. For a routine you can repeat, try our shopping savings checklist.

title: How to save money shopping: a before-you-buy checklist
description: A practical shopping checklist: set a target price, compare products and unit costs, check deal conditions, and avoid buying more than you need.
summary: To save money shopping, decide what you need before looking at deals, compare the total cost of equivalent products, and buy only the quantity you will use. A price comparison helps you choose between purchases; skipping an unnecessary purchase keeps the whole amount unspent.

sections.title: 1. Set the purchase and your target price first
sections.html:
Write down the problem you need to solve: replacing broken headphones, buying a winter coat, or restocking a household product. Then choose the features that matter and the most you are comfortable spending.

That short note gives you a test for tempting offers. If a discounted item does not solve the original problem, it is a new purchase to consider separately. You do not need to turn every sale into a buying decision.

sections.title: 2. Compare equivalent products and quantities
sections.html:
For an exact product, match the model and condition. For consumables you are happy to substitute, compare the cost per unit as well as the pack price.

Imagine a 500 mL bottle costs $8 and a 750 mL bottle of the same product costs $10. The first is $1.60 per 100 mL; the second is about $1.33 per 100 mL. The larger bottle has a lower unit price, but still requires $2 more at checkout. These are example prices.

The larger size only helps if you will use the extra amount and have room to store it. A low unit price is not useful when the surplus goes unused. For products with different concentrations, compare usable doses rather than bottle size alone.

sections.title: 3. Test the conditions of the deal
sections.html:
A free-shipping threshold can turn a small order into a bigger one. If shipping is $6 and you add an unnecessary $15 item to avoid it, you spend $9 more overall. Add something only when you already intended to buy it and the combined order makes sense.

Apply the same logic to multi-buy offers and memberships. Calculate the cost for the amount you need today. If a membership is required, include its cost when deciding whether that particular purchase saves money.

sections.title: 4. Make a quick check before checkout
sections.html:
• Is this the item or specification I planned to buy?
  • Have I checked another available offer for the same product?
  • Does my comparison include delivery and other checkout costs?
  • Will I use everything in this pack or bundle?
  • Would I still want it without the sale sign?

For an unplanned purchase, step away long enough to check those answers. You can make a note of the product and price without committing to it.

sections.title: 5. Make price checks easier while you shop
sections.html:
OLMA helps start a comparison from a product or price-tag photo. It is useful when you are standing in a store and want context before heading to checkout. Verify the matched item and final retailer price before making your decision.

Start with our guide to comparing prices from a photo. If the shelf is full of discount signs, use the sale-price checklist to separate a large advertised discount from a competitive offer.

title: Is duty-free cheaper? How to compare before you buy
description: Compare duty-free and home prices using the same product size and currency. Check the final cost before deciding whether an airport offer is worth it.
summary: Duty-free is not automatically the cheapest option. Compare the exact product and quantity with an available offer at home, convert both to the same currency, and account for costs or restrictions relevant to your trip before buying.

sections.title: Match the product before comparing currencies
sections.html:
An airport offer can look attractive when the number on the shelf is smaller than the price you remember from home. First check whether those numbers describe the same product. Travel sets, different bottle sizes, and regional electronics models can make two offers difficult to compare.

For fragrance, match the concentration as well as the name and volume. For skincare, check the formulation and pack count. For electronics, compare the complete model identifier and included accessories. A similar name is not enough.

sections.title: Put both offers in one currency
sections.html:
Use a conversion rate relevant to your payment method and allow for any applicable payment fees. A price shown by a comparison tool can give you context; the amount charged by your payment provider is what determines your actual cost.

Suppose a fictional airport item costs €60 and your comparison uses an illustrative rate of $1.10 per euro. That is $66 before additional costs. If the identical item is available at home for $64 on comparable terms, the airport offer is already $2 more expensive. If it is $75 at home, the starting difference is $9 in the airport's favor.

Neither result is a live exchange rate or a current product offer. The point is to convert first, then compare. A small apparent saving can disappear when the costs differ.

sections.title: Use unit prices for different pack sizes
sections.html:
When the same formulation comes in different sizes, divide the converted price by the volume. A fictional 100 mL bottle at $66 costs $0.66 per mL. A 75 mL bottle at $54 costs $0.72 per mL. The larger bottle is cheaper per mL but costs $12 more in total.

Choose based on how much you actually want, not just the lower unit price. A travel-exclusive set also deserves a check: assign value only to the items you would otherwise buy.

sections.title: Check the practical cost of bringing it home
sections.html:
Consider luggage space, compatibility, warranty service, and how a return would work after your flight. Before purchasing, check current customs requirements with the destination's official customs authority and baggage rules with your airline. Rules depend on the route and goods, so a price comparison alone cannot settle those questions.

If you cannot establish the exact match or final cost before boarding, you can leave the purchase for later. Airport time pressure does not make an uncertain deal better.
